topic: The Trinity of Logic: Ternary, Towers, and Triangles
target_audience: Undergraduate Computer Science or Mathematics students

sections.title: Foundation: The Power of Three (Ternary)
sections.content: Introduce the Base-3 (ternary) counting system. Explain how each digit represents a state (0, 1, or 2) and how position indicates magnitude ($3^0, 3^1, 3^2$). This serves as the 'coordinate system' for the entire lesson.
sections.example: Visualize a 3-state light switch: 'Off' (0), 'Dim' (1), and 'Bright' (2). Counting from 0 to 8 in ternary (000 to 222) represents all possible configurations of 3 such switches.

sections.title: The Rule Change: Constrained Towers of Hanoi
sections.content: Introduce the 'Linear' or 'Constrained' Towers of Hanoi. Unlike the classic version, disks can only move between ADJACENT pegs (Peg 0 ↔ Peg 1 ↔ Peg 2). To move from Peg 0 to Peg 2, a disk must stop at Peg 1 first. This constraint forces a specific, recursive path.
sections.example: Imagine three rooms in a line (Living Room, Hallway, Bedroom). You cannot teleport a heavy sofa from the Living Room to the Bedroom; it must pass through the Hallway.

sections.title: Mapping States to Geometry
sections.content: Define a 'State' as the position of $n$ disks. Represent every possible valid configuration of disks as a vertex (dot) on a graph. Connect vertices with lines if a single legal move can transition one state to another. This transforms a logic puzzle into a geometric map.
sections.example: With 1 disk, the map is a simple line: State [0]—[1]—[2]. With 2 disks, the map starts to branch, forming small triangles.

sections.title: Emergence of the Sierpinski Triangle
sections.content: Demonstrate that as the number of disks ($n$) increases, the state-space graph of the constrained Hanoi puzzle perfectly forms a Sierpinski Triangle. Each larger triangle is composed of three smaller versions of itself, representing the placement of the largest disk on Peg 0, 1, or 2.
sections.example: Zoom out from a 1-disk line to a 3-disk fractal. Show that the 'corners' of the Sierpinski Triangle represent all disks stacked on a single peg (000, 111, or 222 in ternary).

sections.title: Fractal Traversal via Ternary Addresses
sections.content: Synthesize the concepts. Show how a ternary number acts as a 'GPS address' to find any state on the Sierpinski Triangle. Traversing the edges of the triangle is equivalent to solving the puzzle. The longest path (from Peg 0 to Peg 2) follows the outer boundary of the fractal.
sections.example: A digital ant needs to move from the 'All-on-0' corner to the 'All-on-2' corner. By following the ternary sequence (000 → 001 → ... → 222), the ant traces the zig-zag perimeter of the Sierpinski gasket.
